```{=latex}
\vspace*{-1.6em}
{\color{harvardcrimson}\fontsize{26}{30}\selectfont\bfseries Statistical Learning\par}
\vspace{1pt}
{\large\color{stattextmuted} Can we teach a computer to tell an open book from a closed one?\par}
\vspace{10pt}
Name: \fillline{6.4cm} \hfill Team: \fillline{5.6cm}\par
\vspace{8pt}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  step/.style={signal, signal to=east, signal from=west, draw=none,
    fill=#1, text=white, font=\bfseries\small,
    minimum height=0.8cm, minimum width=3.1cm, inner xsep=4pt},
  node distance=0.08cm]
\node[step=harvardcrimson, signal from=nowhere] (s1) {1. Draw};
\node[step=harvardcrimson!80!black, right=of s1] (s2) {2. Pixelate};
\node[step=tealaccent, right=of s2] (s3) {3. Train};
\node[step=slateaccent, right=of s3] (s4) {4. Test};
\node[step=emeraldaccent, right=of s4] (s5) {5. Evaluate};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
\vspace{-4pt}

\begin{stepbox}{harvardcrimson}{Steps 1 \& 2: Draw, then pixelate}
\textbf{Draw} the object on the slide in \textbf{15 seconds}. Don't show your
teammates yet. Then \textbf{pixelate}: shade every square that has any pencil
mark in it, even a tiny one.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.74cm, y=0.74cm]
  \fill[softteal!45] (0,0) rectangle (16,9);
  \draw[gridblue, line width=0.35pt] (0,0) grid (16,9);
  \draw[tealaccent, line width=1.4pt] (0,0) rectangle (16,9);
  \foreach \l [count=\i] in {a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h,i,j,k,l,m,n,o,p}
    \node[font=\scriptsize\sffamily, text=stattextmuted] at (\i-0.5, 9.32) {\l};
  \foreach \r in {1,...,9}
    \node[font=\scriptsize\sffamily, text=stattextmuted] at (-0.32, 9.5-\r) {\r};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
\vspace{-6pt}
{\small\color{stattextmuted} A computer does not see a picture. It sees a
grid of $16 \times 9 = 144$ squares, each one \textit{shaded} (1) or
\textit{empty} (0).\par}
\end{stepbox}

\begin{stepbox}{tealaccent}{Step 3: Train your algorithm}
Look at your team's pixelated drawings (your \textbf{training data}). Write
rules a computer could follow to decide whether a drawing is an
\textbf{open} or a \textbf{closed} book. Use only the squares: no
``it looks like\dots''

\vspace{10pt}
\textbf{Algorithm name:} \fillline{8.5cm}

\vspace{12pt}
\textbf{Rule 1:} \hrulefill

\vspace{12pt}
\textbf{Rule 2:} \hrulefill

\vspace{12pt}
\textbf{Rule 3:} \hrulefill

\vspace{12pt}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=softteal, colframe=softteal, arc=2pt,
  left=6pt, right=6pt, top=6pt, bottom=6pt]
\textbf{Decision:} \texttt{if} \fillline{8.4cm} \texttt{then} predict
\textbf{open},\\[3pt]
\phantom{\textbf{Decision:} }\texttt{else} predict \textbf{closed}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{stepbox}

\newpage

\begin{stepbox}{slateaccent}{Step 4: Test your algorithm on new drawings}
You will see 10 drawings your team has never seen (the \textbf{testing data}).
Apply your rules \textit{exactly as written} and circle the prediction. Then
circle the actual class and mark whether you were correct.
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\begin{tabular}{>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{1.4cm}
                >{\centering\arraybackslash}p{4.1cm}
                >{\centering\arraybackslash}p{4.1cm}
                >{\centering\arraybackslash}p{2.4cm}}
\rowcolor{slateaccent}
\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Image}} &
\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Predicted class}} &
\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Actual class}} &
\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Correct?}} \\
1  & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
\rowcolor{slateaccent!8}
2  & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
3  & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
\rowcolor{slateaccent!8}
4  & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
5  & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
\rowcolor{slateaccent!8}
6  & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
7  & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
\rowcolor{slateaccent!8}
8  & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
9  & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
\rowcolor{slateaccent!8}
10 & open \qquad closed & open \qquad closed & yes \quad no \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\vspace{-4pt}
\end{stepbox}

\begin{stepbox}{emeraldaccent}{Step 5: Evaluate your model}
Count how many of the 10 test images land in each cell. We call
\textbf{open} the \textit{positive} class.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=5.0cm, y=1.45cm,
  cell/.style={minimum width=4.85cm, minimum height=1.35cm, align=center,
    rounded corners=2pt, line width=0.8pt},
  head/.style={font=\bfseries\small, align=center}]
  \node[head] at (1,0.7) {Predicted: OPEN};
  \node[head] at (2,0.7) {Predicted: CLOSED};
  \node[head, anchor=east] at (0.5,0) {Actual: OPEN};
  \node[head, anchor=east] at (0.5,-1) {Actual: CLOSED};
  \node[cell, fill=softgreen, draw=emeraldaccent] at (1,0)
    {\textcolor{emeraldaccent}{\textbf{True Positive (TP)}}\\[5pt] \fillline{1.4cm}};
  \node[cell, fill=softorange, draw=orangeaccent] at (2,0)
    {\textcolor{orangeaccent}{\textbf{False Negative (FN)}}\\[5pt] \fillline{1.4cm}};
  \node[cell, fill=softcrimson, draw=harvardcrimson] at (1,-1)
    {\textcolor{harvardcrimson}{\textbf{False Positive (FP)}}\\[5pt] \fillline{1.4cm}};
  \node[cell, fill=softgreen, draw=emeraldaccent] at (2,-1)
    {\textcolor{emeraldaccent}{\textbf{True Negative (TN)}}\\[5pt] \fillline{1.4cm}};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
\vspace{-2pt}
\textbf{Accuracy} $= \dfrac{\text{TP} + \text{TN}}{\text{total}} =
\dfrac{\rule{1.2cm}{0.5pt}}{10} = $ \fillline{1.8cm}
\end{stepbox}

\begin{stepbox}{harvardcrimson}{Discuss with your team}
\textbf{(a)} A medical test predicts \textit{disease} or \textit{no disease}.
Which is worse here, a false positive or a false negative? Why?

\vspace{1.0cm}
\textbf{(b)} Your rules worked on your own team's drawings. Why might they do
worse on new drawings? What do we call a model that fits its training data
\textit{too} well?

\vspace{1.0cm}
\end{stepbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=softcrimson, colframe=softcrimson, arc=3pt,
  left=8pt, right=8pt, top=4pt, bottom=4pt, before skip=2pt]
\small\linespread{1.05}\selectfont
\textbf{Algorithm:} the recipe (a set of rules). \quad
\textbf{Model:} the algorithm after it is trained on data. \quad
\textbf{Training data:} the data the model learns from. \quad
\textbf{Testing data:} new data we check the model on.\\[2pt]
\textit{``All models are wrong, but some are useful.''} (George Box)
\end{tcolorbox}
```
